rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the 22-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing late compounds. The midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Test temperature selectivity while keeping the gradient fixed, targeting the late coelution and other underresolved pairs. Higher temperature should also provide time margin for a shallower gradient if needed.

Compare directly with injection 1 to determine which critical pairs respond to gradient slope, especially the late coelution that persisted at higher temperature. The steeper gradient also creates room to explore lower temperatures without a time penalty.

Lower temperature should improve the early critical pair, while a shallower gradient may improve the slope-sensitive middle pairs. Raising the starting organic fraction offsets added retention time and tests whether the early peaks tolerate trimming the gradient window.

Use a narrower, shallower gradient to spread the underresolved middle and late pairs while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes. The early peaks in injection 4 retain enough separation to justify testing a higher starting organic fraction.

Retain the shallower slope from injection 5 but lower the starting organic fraction to improve the marginal early and middle separations. A moderate temperature increase should help the pair near 5.8 minutes while keeping the last peak close to 10 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient near the best region, using a higher starting fraction to keep the last peak near 10 minutes. Moving to 30 C should strengthen the temperature-sensitive late separations without sacrificing too much resolution in the middle cluster.

Test whether placing the late cluster in the final hold improves the persistent near-coelution, which has barely responded to temperature or gradient slope. This moderate final organic fraction should limit the delay of the last peak while probing a different selectivity regime.

Return to the promising gradient from injection 6 and isolate the effect of lowering temperature. This should improve the early and late critical separations while keeping the last peak near the 10-minute threshold.

Lower the temperature of injection 7 to strengthen the remaining middle and late critical pairs. This combines its shallower gradient with the favorable selectivity at 25 C, with the last peak expected very close to 10 minutes.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower slope to improve the remaining middle and late separations while targeting a last peak near 10 minutes. This also establishes whether compression of the early peaks limits further window trimming.

Explore a substantially shifted, shallower gradient to test for a better selectivity region beyond the current local optimum. This may separate the persistent late doublet, though compression and reordering of early peaks are the main risks.

Refine around injection 7 with a slightly shallower slope, aiming to improve the three remaining underresolved pairs. The predicted last peak is close to 10 minutes, so this tests the resolution–time boundary without a large expected time penalty.

Lower the starting fraction relative to the best method to test whether improved middle-pair selectivity outweighs the accompanying increase in slope. This probes the lower-window side of the optimum while keeping the predicted last peak close to 10 minutes.

Test a slope between injections 5 and 10, keeping the favorable low-temperature selectivity but bringing the last peak safely below 10 minutes. This checks whether avoiding the time penalty preserves enough resolution to improve the best score.

Test one more shallow-slope refinement near injection 13 to quantify whether gains in the remaining critical pairs outweigh a small time penalty. This brackets the resolution–time optimum at a starting fraction that still preserves the early separations.

Place the final hold just after the late critical cluster, using a slope close to the best narrow-window method. This tests whether the gradient-to-hold transition improves late selectivity without pushing the last peak substantially beyond 10 minutes.

Bracket the temperature optimum between injections 9 and 6 while retaining the best gradient. This checks whether a modest selectivity shift can improve the persistent late doublet without losing too much middle-pair resolution.

Test an intermediate slope between injections 4 and 14, aiming to retain their favorable middle-pair selectivity while bringing the last peak below 10 minutes. This probes a remaining low-temperature candidate near the resolution–time boundary.

Complete the low-temperature comparison for injection 13, testing whether improved middle and late resolution compensates for a modest time penalty. This directly brackets the shallower-slope side of the best 25 C methods.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 11 to recover its marginal middle separations and improve the late cluster. This probes whether those gains can offset the early-pair deficit while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

Test the original broad gradient at the most favorable temperature, checking whether the lower starting fraction improves middle-pair selectivity enough to challenge the current best. The last peak is expected near 10 minutes, limiting the likely time penalty.
Refine the steeper side of injection 10 with a last peak expected below 10 minutes. This tests whether eliminating its small time penalty can compensate for the modest loss of resolution.

Test the steeper neighbor of the best method at the same starting fraction and temperature. This checks whether the critical-pair pattern improves with a modest slope change while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test a slope between injections 19 and 14, targeting improved middle-pair resolution with the last peak near 10 minutes. The final hold begins after the critical late cluster, preserving its gradient separation while testing the remaining resolution–time boundary.
